name: Japanese Chestnut at Saint John the Apostle

location.address: Saint John the Apostle Catholic Church grounds, 101 Oakcrest Manor Dr NE, Leesburg, VA 20176

official_register.name: Loudoun County Big Tree Registry (Dept of Building & Development, Forest Resources; measured 2025)

access: Church grounds and parish cemetery beside Church Street NE, Leesburg. The county flags this tree as visible or accessible from public property. Check for services or funerals before walking in; no published hours.
transport: Downtown Leesburg; Loudoun County Transit stop Union St and King St is about a 3 minute walk (OSM stop ref 29).

location_site.name: Saint John the Apostle church grounds and cemetery, Church Street NE

verify_notes: Virginia Tech Big Tree record 2457 (nominated by Robert Vickers, 2015): Japanese chestnut, 161 in girth, 45 ft, crown 40 ft, status 'legacy', not a Virginia champion; land owner St. John the Apostle Catholic Church; GPS 39.11885,-77.56139; 'just north of a spring house at a sharp turn of Church Street, entering the grounds from the south'. Identification was hard: Virginia Tech first said Castanea sativa; The American Chestnut Foundation concluded Castanea crenata, partly because the tree is 'very aged' and shows no chestnut blight. Loudoun County registry remeasured 2025: 171 in (434 cm), 54 ft (16.5 m), crown 55 ft, marked Virginia champion in the county list (VT record says not champion, conflict between the two, not resolved). Alive: measured 2025 by the county. No age given by any source; left empty. Trees lsb_001 and lsb_004 stand about 7 m apart; lsb_001 to lsb_004 are the four registered trees on this one site. Photo candidate: none looked for. Figures from county feature layer (girth in inches 171 x 2.54), PDF cross-checked.

verify_notes: Loudoun County registry 2025 (PDF row, cols corrected): 103 ft (31.4 m), 201 in girth (511 cm), crown 69 ft, 321 points; the feature layer row is column-shifted. An older write-up of the Oatlands ginkgo (Atlas Obscura, via search result only, page 403) quoted 82 ft and 185 in; the figures differ, the 2025 county ones are used. Middleburg Life (Jim Donegan, Oatlands' tree contractor): 'third largest ginkgo in the country', 'close to 200 years old', Virginia Tech measured it (the arborist's age claim, no core cited). ALIVE CAVEAT: the county forester's July 2026 visit to Oatlands found the nearby American hornbeam (VT record 1457) REMOVED; the ginkgo was not reported removed, but nobody has confirmed it since 2025. Writer or later pass should confirm with Oatlands (703-727-0670) before publishing. Pin: registry coordinate, 'behind the mansion'; approximate. The hornbeam is dead/removed: rejected. Estate also has a 200-year-old American boxwood canopy near the picnic tables and 200-year-old yews per the same article (not individually pinned).

name: Leesburg Heritage Tree
age_estimate: well over 250 years, by the town

location.address: Ida Lee Park, beside the Rust Farm House, 50 Ida Lee Drive NW, Leesburg, VA 20176

access: Ida Lee Park is a free town park. The tree is next to the Rust Farm House beside the festival field.
transport: About 1.2 km north-west of downtown Leesburg; roughly 15 minutes on foot. No bus checked.

location_site.name: Rust Farm House yard, Ida Lee Park

verify_notes: Source: the Town of Leesburg Tree Commission's 'Tree Walk of Historic Leesburg' leaflet (read through a Wayback copy): 'Leesburg Heritage Tree' is 'a fine specimen of a Northern White Oak that is well over 250 years old and grew from a seed before the Town of Leesburg was founded in 1758'; located 'next to Rust Farm House, circa 1859 (50 Ida Lee Drive NW)'. Age is the town's statement, no core or measurement cited. Pin is the farmhouse address point (39.12406,-77.56477, Nominatim/OSM), not the trunk; no tree node with species in OSM; no girth. The town's America 250 page says the park 'once' had several mature white oaks and planted a Mount Vernon chestnut oak sapling beside the farmhouse in May 2026 (do not confuse the sapling with the heritage oak). A Loudoun Times piece of 23 Jan 2026 reports the town's tree inventory measuring a 'massive white oak' at Ida Lee Park (arborist Jack Myrna; article text paywalled, not read, not necessarily the same tree). Alive: not confirmed since the leaflet (leaflet undated, archive copy Jan 2026); the 2026 article suggests a large white oak stands there. Flagged: single source, pin is a site.
